claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix are prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation.
A thin, uniform Ni coating should be deposited on the tungsten surfaces before composite consolidation.
The deposited Ni will form an interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
A Ni interlayer at the W–Cu interface will act as a diffusion barrier.
The Ni interlayer will improve wetting between tungsten and copper.
The Ni interlayer will improve structural matching between tungsten and copper.
The Ni coating will reduce interdiffusion at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating will reduce lattice-mismatch stresses at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni coating will form a stable, low-energy W–Ni–Cu interface.
The Ni coating will minimize phase separation during consolidation or service.
The Ni coating will reduce interfacial void formation.
Reducing phase separation and void formation will preserve heat-conduction pathways under elevated-temperature and irradiation conditions.
A Ni-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical untreated W–Cu composite.
A Ni-coated W–Cu composite will have better interfacial integrity than an untreated W–Cu composite.
Interfacial voids and phase separation in untreated W–Cu composites degrade thermal conductivity under high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The proposed benefit applies only when Ni deposition is sufficiently uniform and the Ni layer remains intact during service.
Severe irradiation or thermal excursions may degrade the Ni layer and limit its effectiveness.
The thermal-conductivity improvement and long-term stability may depend on Ni coating thickness, coating uniformity, and processing parameters.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity and thermal conductivity, or failure to reduce void formation and phase separation, would falsify the hypothesis.
